Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
make sure to stay close to exit
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
issues.explanation: This item is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the cognitive formulation. The active formulation is dominated by a Triggers–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Negative Appraisals inactive. In contrast, punishment/self-deserving-suffering is a negative self-appraisal theme rather than a threat-management strategy, and it does not connect plausibly to the selected trigger and threat items. The other maladaptive strategies (avoiding emotional stress, staying near exits) fit the trigger-threat-hypervigilance pattern, but punishment thinking pulls toward a different clinical profile that is otherwise not represented.

vignette: Carlos had spent the first thirty years of his life in uniform, marching through deserts and training under the relentless glare of artillery fire. The day that changed him was a sudden mortar strike during a nighttime exercise in the Middle East. He was standing in the trench when the concussive shockwave tore through the mud, sending shards of concrete into the air. The sound was a low, bone-shaking boom, and when he turned to see the aftermath, he saw a comrade's blood splattered on his face, the taste of metal and burnt plastic in his mouth, and a dizzy, light-headed haze that swallowed his vision. He had never imagined that a single taste or the flutter of a heart could leave a permanent echo in his mind. Years later, as he teaches a class of students with severe learning disabilities, those memories come back in a very particular way. The first trigger he feels is a sudden dizziness, as if the ground is tilting, whenever he hears a student shout or when the fluorescent lights flicker. The metallic taste lingers in his mouth if he thinks of the mortar shell's impact, and even simply talking about the incident-whether to a colleague or his estranged wife-sets a ripple of unease across his body. These sensations force him into a defensive posture. He immediately checks his surroundings, his gaze darting to the doors, the windows, the corners of the room, looking for any sign that the same fate could unfold. The sense of threat that rises from the taste or the dizziness, in turn, makes him plan escape routes before he even feels comfortable in the classroom. He always knows, with a cold certainty, where the nearest exit lies and how long it would take him to get there. He stays close to that exit, keeping a few extra steps between himself and the front of the room, because he is certain that if the threat were to reappear, he would need to flee quickly. Each time he feels the threat in a sudden, unexpected sound-a distant siren or the hiss of the school's ventilation-his heart hammers, his eyes widen, and the hypervigilance he has cultivated becomes almost physical. That hypervigilance itself triggers the dizziness he first recalls; the cycle feeds back on itself, each iteration tightening the loop. The pattern has not stayed contained to the classroom. In meetings with his department head, he avoids topics that stir strong emotions-such as curriculum changes or student progress reports-preferring instead to remain in the safety of routine and routine structure. His avoidance of emotional stress, a self-prescribed protective strategy, only heightens his sense of threat; the more he evades confronting difficult emotions, the more anxious he feels about them, and the more he scans the room for any sign of danger. The constant checking and staying near the exit have become an all-day habit: he walks around the classroom with a mind that maps every possible exit and with a body that feels ready to bolt. It has begun to show in his work. He missed a staff meeting because he feared the noise of the projector might trigger an unexpected sound; his assistant complained that he seemed distracted, that he was "in a hurry" or "too nervous." His students sense his tension; his ability to connect with them has weakened, and their progress stalls. Carlos has lived with this loop for months, each day a repetition of triggers, threat, avoidance, and new threats born from his own vigilance. The sense that he is trapped in a never-ending cycle of fear has taken a heavy toll. He realized, on a Thursday afternoon, that he was so exhausted by the constant scanning that he could no longer focus on the student who needed him most. When a boy's sudden outburst filled the room with noise, Carlos felt a sharp, dizzy throb rise in his chest, and the metallic taste returned with an almost physical intensity. He stared at the nearest exit, then turned back to the boy, knowing he would have to flee if the noise grew louder. That moment, when he thought he might have to abandon the classroom in a heartbeat, pushed him to the edge. He left the school early, walked home under the evening sky, and stared at his reflection in the storefront window. He could no longer deny that the thought of losing his job, of letting his students down, filled him with terror. It was this fear-of losing his place, of losing his purpose-that finally compelled him to seek help. He hopes that by understanding the roots of his reactions, he can find a way to break the chain, to reduce the dizziness and taste that haunt him, and to regain the calm he once felt in the classroom and in life.
